q-213407.name: Question 1
q-213407.problem:
Which of the following integers has a multiplicative inverse modulo $27?$

- $11$
- $16$
- $23$
q-213407.worked_solution:
An integer $a$ has a multiplicative inverse modulo $n$ if and only if $a$ and $n$ are coprime, i.e., $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1.$

With this in mind, let's examine the given options.

- $11$ has a multiplicative inverse modulo $27$ since $\text{gcd}(11,27)=1.\,\,✓$

- $16$ has a multiplicative inverse modulo $27$ since $\text{gcd}(16,27)=1.\,\,✓$

- $23$ has a multiplicative inverse modulo $27$ since $\text{gcd}(23,27)=1.\,\,✓$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

q-213405.problem:
Which of the following integers has a multiplicative inverse modulo $36?$

- $5$
- $13$
- $24$
q-213405.worked_solution:
An integer $a$ has a multiplicative inverse modulo $n$ if and only if $a$ and $n$ are coprime, i.e., $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1.$

With this in mind, let's examine the given options.

- $5$ has a multiplicative inverse modulo $36$ since $\text{gcd}(5,36)=1.\,\,✓$

- $13$ has a multiplicative inverse modulo $36$ since $\text{gcd}(13,36)=1.\,\,✓$

- $24$ does *not* have a multiplicative inverse modulo $36$ since $\text{gcd}(24,36)=12\ne 1.\,\,\times $

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

q-213441.name: Question 3
q-213441.worked_solution:
The multiplicative inverse of $3$ modulo $11,$ denoted ${3}^{-1},$ is the number $x$ such that

$$
3\cdot x≡1\,(\text{mod}\,11).
$$

Note that since $\text{gcd}(3,11)=1,$ an inverse element exists and is unique up to congruence modulo $11.$

Since the modulus $n=11$ is small, we can find the inverse $x$ by computing exponents of $3$ (modulo $11$) until we get a result of $1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{2} & ≡3\cdot 3≡9 &  & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ {3}^{3} & ≡3\cdot 9≡27≡2\cdot 11+5≡5 &  & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ {3}^{4} & ≡3\cdot 5≡15≡11+4≡4 &  & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ {3}^{5} & ≡3\cdot 4≡12≡11+1≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,11)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $3\cdot 4≡1\,(\text{mod}\,11).$ Therefore, the multiplicative inverse of $3$ modulo $11$ is $4.$

q-213414.name: Question 4
q-213414.worked_solution:
The multiplicative inverse of $3$ modulo $5,$ denoted ${3}^{-1},$ is the number $x$ such that

$$
3\cdot x≡1\,(\text{mod}\,5).
$$

Note that since $\text{gcd}(3,5)=1,$ an inverse element exists and is unique up to congruence modulo $5.$

Since the modulus $n=5$ is small, we can find the inverse $x$ by computing exponents of $3$ (modulo $5$) until we get a result of $1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{2} & ≡3\cdot 3≡9≡5+4≡4 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ {3}^{3} & ≡3\cdot 4≡12≡2\cdot 5+2≡2 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ {3}^{4} & ≡3\cdot 2≡6≡5+1≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $3\cdot 2≡1\,(\text{mod}\,5).$ Therefore, the multiplicative inverse of $3$ modulo $5$ is $2.$

q-213532.worked_solution:
First of all, notice that $\text{gcd}(50,97)=1.$ So, the multiplicative inverse of $50$ modulo $97$ exists.

The multiplicative inverse of $50$ modulo $97$ is the number $x$ such that

$$
50\cdot x≡1\,(\text{mod}\,97).
$$

To find the value of $x,$ we will use the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}97 & = & 50\cdot 1 & + & 47 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 50 & = & 47\cdot 1 & + & 3 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 47 & = & 3\cdot 15 & + & 2 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 3 & = & 2\cdot 1 & + & 1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Solving for the rightmost terms in the equations above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}47 & =97-50 \\ 3 & =50-47 \\ 2 & =47-3\cdot 15 \\ 1 & =3-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we back-substitute:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =3-2 \\  & =3-(47-3\cdot 15) \\  & =3\cdot 16-47 \\  & =(50-47)\cdot 16-47 \\  & =50\cdot 16-47\cdot 17 \\  & =50\cdot 16-(97-50)\cdot 17 \\  & =50\cdot 33-97\cdot 17 \\  & =50\cdot 33+97\cdot (-17)\end{aligned}
$$

We can write this result modulo $97,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}50\cdot 33+97\cdot (-17) & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,97) \\ 50\cdot 33 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,97)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $50\cdot 33≡1\,(\text{mod}\,97),$ which means that ${50}^{-1}\,\text{mod}\,97=33.$

The multiplicative inverse of $55$ modulo $258$ is the number $x$ such that

$$
55\cdot x≡1\,(\text{mod}\,258).

To find the value of $x,$ we will use the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}258 & = & 55\cdot 4 & + & 38 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 55 & = & 38\cdot 1 & + & 17 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 38 & = & 17\cdot 2 & + & 4 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 17 & = & 4\cdot 4 & + & 1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Solving for the rightmost terms in the equations above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}38 & =258-55\cdot 4 \\ 17 & =55-38 \\ 4 & =38-17\cdot 2 \\ 1 & =17-4\cdot 4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we back-substitute:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =17-4\cdot 4 \\  & =17-(38-17\cdot 2)\cdot 4 \\  & =17\cdot 9-38\cdot 4 \\  & =(55-38)\cdot 9-38\cdot 4 \\  & =55\cdot 9-38\cdot 13 \\  & =55\cdot 9-(258-55\cdot 4)\cdot 13 \\  & =55\cdot 61+258\cdot (-13)\end{aligned}
$$

We can write this result modulo $258,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}55\cdot 61+258\cdot (-13) & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,258) \\ 55\cdot 61 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,258)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $55\cdot 61≡1\,(\text{mod}\,258),$ which means that ${55}^{-1}\,\text{mod}\,258=61.$
